note: Apollo 11 facts were checked against the approved NASA NSSDCA Lunar Module and CSM records and NASA's Apollo 11 anniversary page. Illustrative staging is documented in DECISIONS.md.

facts.text: The Apollo 11 Lunar Module descent stage contained storage space for lunar equipment and experiments.
EASEP was deployed approximately 17 m south of the Lunar Module before it was turned on by ground command.
EASEP was turned on by ground command at 04:40:39 UT on 21 July 1969 while the astronauts were still on the lunar surface.
EASEP had two solar panels that provided power, and it could operate only during lunar day. The panels faced east and west.
Aldrin returned to the Lunar Module first. Armstrong followed at 05:09:32 UT after transferring sample boxes to Aldrin and placing a packet of memorial items on the ground.
The extravehicular activity ended at 05:11:13 UT when the Lunar Module hatch was closed.
Apollo 11 launched on 16 July 1969, entered Earth orbit, used the S-IVB for translunar injection, docked Columbia with Eagle, coasted to the Moon, entered lunar orbit, and returned to Earth.
facts.sourceName: NASA NSSDCA: Apollo 11 Command and Service Module

facts.text: Apollo 11 launched on a Saturn V from Kennedy Space Center at 13:32 UT on 16 July 1969. The S-IVB translunar injection burn lasted 5 minutes 48 seconds.
facts.sourceName: NASA NSSDCA: Apollo 11 Command and Service Module

facts.text: The Command and Service Module mass was 28,801 kg; the Service Module main engine thrust was about 91,000 N. Columbia remained in lunar orbit while Eagle was on the surface and returned the crew to Earth.
facts.sourceName: NASA NSSDCA: Apollo 11 Command and Service Module

facts.text: The Lunar Module ascent stage had a dry mass of 2,445 kg, carried 2,376 kg of propellant, was about 2.8 m high, had a 6.65 m3 crew compartment with no seats, used an ascent engine with about 15,000 N thrust, and lifted off on 21 July 1969.

The Lunar Module descent stage was 4.2 m across and 1.7 m thick; its four landing legs held it 1.5 m above the surface with 9.4 m between opposite footpads. Its descent engine could throttle down for landing, and the stage remained on the Moon.
The astronauts collected 21.55 kg of lunar rock and soil and traversed about 250 m on the lunar surface.

The Apollo 11 astronauts deployed a flag and a lunar surface television camera, spoke with the U.S. President by radio, unveiled a plaque mounted on a strut, and took a photograph reflecting the photographer and Lunar Module in an astronaut's visor.

EASEP had a mass of 48 kg, two solar panels, a passive seismometer, a lunar dust detector, and an antenna and communications system. It received commands at 2119 MHz, sent telemetry at 2276.5 MHz, and was a forerunner of later ALSEP packages.
The laser ranging retroreflector was considered part of EASEP, was not attached to the station, required no power, and was deployed about 5 m north-northwest of EASEP.
Powered descent began at 20:05 UT on 20 July 1969 and lasted 756.3 seconds.
The Lunar Module landed in the Sea of Tranquility at 20:17:40 UT on 20 July 1969.
Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface at 02:56:15 UT on 21 July 1969; Aldrin followed 19 minutes later. This was more than six hours after landing.
NASA's Apollo 11 anniversary page records Collins saying, "You cats take it easy on the lunar surface," and the landing call, "The Eagle has landed."
The Lunar Module ascent stage lifted off at 17:54:01 UT on 21 July after 21 hours 36 minutes on the lunar surface, docked with Columbia, and was jettisoned into lunar orbit.
The flag was knocked over when the Lunar Module lifted off, and after docking the lunar samples were brought aboard the Command Module.
Apollo 11 splashed down in the Pacific Ocean at 16:50:35 UT on 24 July 1969.
facts.sourceName: NASA NSSDCA: Apollo 11 Command and Service Module

facts.text: EASEP transmission stopped by ground command about five hours before lunar sunset on 3 August 1969. It was turned on again the next lunar day.
EASEP operated normally despite temperatures 30 C above its planned maximum; near noon of its second lunar day on 27 August 1969, it no longer accepted commands and the experiment was terminated.
The Apollo 11 astronauts' lunar footprints may last millions of years barring a chance meteorite impact.
